C0.quote: unanimous and strategy-proof random rules on these domains
C0.note: Strategy-proof random social choice functions aggregating agents' preferences; a strategic property of voting rules.

C1.quote: if and only if it is a TRM rule
C1.note: Characterization of unanimous and strategy-proof RSCFs. The main results are axiomatic, with strategy-proofness as a property.

C2.1.quote: A preference profile, denoted by PN = (P1 , . . . , Pn )

C2.2.quote: complete, reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive binary relation (also called a linear order)
C2.2.note: Strict rankings for most results; weak preferences with a plateau of at most two at the top in Section 5.

C2.3.quote: based on preferences of individuals in a society
C2.3.note: Preferences are the agents' attitudes, and strategy-proofness refers to misreporting them.

C2.4.quote: misreporting his/her preference will be first order stochastically dominated by the original/sincere outcome
C2.4.note: Strategy-proofness is defined by comparing a true preference Pi against a misreport Pi', so the two are separate objects.

C3.1.quote: strategy-proof if for all i ∈ N, all PN ∈ D n , all Pi′ ∈ D
C3.1.note: All results concern strategy-proofness, which considers misreports.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction or distortion notions are used for voters. Only ordinal preferences appear.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Unanimity is an axiom and not a welfare criterion in the sense of the codebook. No welfare, distortion or representation evaluation appears.

VOT.quote_behav: all Pi′ ∈ D, and all x ∈ A
VOT.note: Agents may deviate to any Pi'; strategy-proofness means no profitable misreport. Information is not specified, although the dominance-based definition holds for any profile of the others.

DES.note: The designer is mentioned only informally, as knowing the top-set (Remark 4.1). The designer's choice or objective is not modelled.

C8.1.quote: An RSCF is strategy-proof if for all i ∈ N
C8.1.note: Strategy-proofness is defined via first-order stochastic dominance, which is a dominant-strategy notion.

C8.2.quote: Our notion of strategy-proofness (which is introduced in Gibbard (1977))

claims.quote: This property can be utilized in finding the optimal RSCFs for a society.
many political and economic scenarios where preferences of individuals satisfy natural restrictions

C9.1.note: The claims about real-world relevance are weak and concern the applicability of the domains.

C9.2.note: The claims about applicability and optimal rules are supported by the formal results and the domain definitions; no unstated modelling assumption is needed.
